First-visit and every-visit

An episode can pass through the same state more than once. First-visit Monte Carlo averages only the return after the first visit in each episode. Every-visit Monte Carlo averages the returns after all of them. Both converge to $v_\pi$, but they are not the same estimator.

Lesson 1's corridor. The flag pays $+10$ and ends the episode, every other step pays $0$, and $\gamma = 0.9$. Walk with the arrows and double back to visit cells twice. Green: first visits. Blue: repeat visits.

Each return from time $t$ is $G_t = 10\,\gamma^{T-t-1}$, where $T$ is the step that reaches the flag. A repeat visit is closer to the end, so its return is larger.

One state, many loops (S&B Exercise 5.5)

⟲ stay
prob $p$, $+1$

prob $1 - p$, $+1$

One state, one action, $\gamma = 1$. An episode of length $T$ visits $s$ at $t = 0, 1, \dots, T-1$ with returns $T, T-1, \dots, 1$. The true value is $v(s) = 1/(1-p)$.

The experiment repeats 3000 times: play $n$ episodes, form both estimates. The lines are the average estimate for each $n$. An unbiased estimator sits on the true value for every $n$.

The maths

Suppose state $s$ is visited at times $t_1 < t_2 < \dots$ in an episode. The two methods differ only in which returns they record:

$$\text{first-visit: } G_{t_1} \qquad\qquad \text{every-visit: } G_{t_1}, G_{t_2}, \dots$$

Each method averages its recorded returns over all episodes.

First-visit is unbiased. Each episode adds at most one return per state. By the Markov property, what happens after the first visit doesn't depend on how you got there, so each recorded return has mean exactly $v_\pi(s)$, and different episodes are independent. The average of $n$ of them has mean $v_\pi(s)$ for every $n$ and standard error $\sigma/\sqrt{n}$.

Every-visit is biased but consistent. Returns from the same episode overlap (here $G_{t_2}$ is a piece of $G_{t_1}$), and long episodes contribute more of them. In the loop machine, one episode of length $T$ gives

$$\hat v_{\text{first}} = T, \qquad \hat v_{\text{every}} = \frac{T + (T-1) + \cdots + 1}{T} = \frac{T+1}{2}$$

Since $\mathbb{E}[T] = 1/(1-p)$, the first-visit estimate has the right mean, while the every-visit estimate from one episode has mean $\tfrac12\big(\tfrac{1}{1-p} + 1\big)$. With $p = 0.9$: $10$ versus $5.5$. Pooled over many episodes, the every-visit average tends to $\mathbb{E}[T(T+1)/2] / \mathbb{E}[T] = 1/(1-p)$, so the bias shrinks to zero (S&B §5.1 notes both methods converge).

Every-visit is natural with function approximation and eligibility traces (Lessons 57–58). For now, first-visit is the default.
